md: AppArmor's manual warns that complain mode "does not provide any security, only auditing" and should not be used in a hostile environment, because an attacker's behaviour would be logged and could be added to the profile as if it were normal. Also remember the runc advisory: CVE-2019-5736 was not blocked by the default AppArmor policy. A profile protects only what it was written to cover.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: A common misconception is that editing a `.h` file only affects the `.cpp` with the same name. The compiler pastes headers into every includer, so `tensor.h` here costs 4 recompiles, not 1.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
md: Node ids, `-k`, `-m` and `--lf` turn a 20 minute suite into a 2 second loop. Use the narrow loop while fixing, then run the wider set CI will run before you push.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Answer every comment, say what you changed, fix the code rather than explaining it in the thread, and thank the reviewer. The kernel guide adds: when you send a new version, list what changed since the previous one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: A CoC is not only about insults. Contributor Covenant 2.1 lists publishing others' private information (an address, an email) without explicit permission as unacceptable, and it covers private harassment too.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: Fixup commits are not magic on their own. If you push `fixup!` commits and never autosquash, a PR merged with a merge commit or with rebase and merge (two of GitHub's merge methods, covered in lesson 5) lands them on main exactly as they are, `fixup!` titles and all. Autosquash before asking for the final merge unless the project says otherwise.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Two common myths: copyleft does not make internal use public (only conveying triggers it), and it does not ban commercial use (you may charge for copies). What it controls is the terms you pass on.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: Common misconception: "the new number is smaller, so the change is faster". Two single measurements differ almost always, even for identical code. Without repeated runs and a test, a 5% gap can be pure noise.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
md: Trace from the specific end toward the general one. Start at the observable string or the command's own handler, search downward through callees, and use a backtrace (or a log line) to bridge function pointers, callbacks and event loops.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: Do not reuse a reducer's interestingness script as a bisect script unchanged. They use opposite conventions: for C-Reduce and llvm-reduce, exit 0 means the bug is *present*; for `git bisect run`, exit 0 means the commit is *good* (bug absent). The inversion silently sends bisect to the wrong commit.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Do not write `Closes #123` on a PR that only partly addresses the issue: merging it will close the issue for everyone. Write "Part of #123" or "Refs #123" (neither is a closing keyword).

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
md: A leaked password or API key found during recon is not an invitation to log in with it. Unless the rules of engagement explicitly allow using discovered credentials, record where it was found and report it at once so it can be rotated.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and just-in-time (JIT) frames differently, where JIT code is machine code that a runtime such as the Java virtual machine compiles while the program runs), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: Privacy engineering reviews every data action, not only every attacker. NIST's objectives give the questions: will people be surprised (predictability), can we find and change or delete one person's data (manageability), and does the system know who is who more than it needs to (disassociability)?

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
md: l-diversity and t-closeness reduce attribute disclosure in one table under one attacker model. They do not compose across releases and they give no guarantee against unanticipated background knowledge.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
md: A published epsilon is a starting point for review, not a verdict. Ask what the unit of privacy is, how the budget is split across tables and geographies, and what error users can tolerate. The Census case shows that both privacy and accuracy are political as well as technical choices.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
md: A DPIA written after launch, or one whose risk section lists only security threats to the company, misses the point. It must be done before processing, assess necessity, and score harm to the individuals in the data.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
md: Misconception: "a context switch costs a few microseconds, so it does not matter." That is the direct cost on an idle cache. Li et al. found the total ranged from several microseconds to more than a thousand, depending on working set size and access pattern. Benchmarks that touch no data hide the part that hurts.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Prompt optimization is search: candidates (instructions and demos), a metric, a dev set to score on, and a proposer. Everything else in this course is a choice of proposer, a way to spend the budget, or a way to keep the final number honest.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
md: More sampling buys you less than independence suggests. Sequence sampling cannot rescue an undesignable backbone, which is why designability of the generator, measured at a fixed small M, is the metric the backbone papers compete on.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: A hash match is strong evidence; a hash miss proves nothing. Security researcher David Bianco's [Pyramid of Pain](https://detect-respond.blogspot.com/2013/03/the-pyramid-of-pain.html) puts hash values at the bottom because changing a single byte gives the attacker a brand new hash. Use hash lists to catch known copies quickly, never as the only control.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT (scale-invariant feature transform) image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Prices, quantities and negative numbers: validating what input means
md: If a value influences price, access, ownership or state, assume the client made it up. Recompute it from server data, and validate every remaining input for business meaning: range, type, and how it combines with the other fields.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Flexcoin and Poloniex, the bitcoin banks that raced (2014)
md: Internal balances are money. A transfer between two users of the same service can drain the service if the debit is not atomic, because every later withdrawal trusts those balances.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: A concurrency test that passes once proves little: races are probabilistic. Use many parallel workers, a barrier so they start together, a real database rather than a mock, and run it on every build so a later refactor that reopens the window is caught.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
md: Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: A crime with a supply chain: the roles and the money
md: Ransomware is a business whose only income is victims who pay. Every victim who can restore without paying lowers the expected value of the next intrusion, and every payment funds it.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Backups that survive an attacker with Domain Admin
md: A backup survives only if the credentials, network and storage that protect it are independent of production identity. Keep at least one copy immutable in a separate account or offline, back up AD and the rebuild tooling too, and time real restores.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: A short timeout detects dead peers fast but turns a transient congestion spike into a fatal QP error; a long one can stall an application for seconds. Pick it from your fabric's real round-trip and queueing delays, not from habit.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
md: Bandwidth is set by what changes, how it is encoded, and how often you send it. Latency under loss is set by the transport: an ordered stream turns one lost packet into a stall for every later update.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: A gap between a random-split number and a temporal-split number is not a bug in either; they measure different tasks. Only the temporal one resembles what the system will face, so compare models on that.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: Aggregation keeps a small state per group. Hashing finds the state with a table (memory grows with groups); sorting brings each group together so one state suffices (needs ordered input). Sort and hash nodes both spill to disk when they exceed their memory limit.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
md: Pick the knobs by the question each one answers: **N** sets how many copies survive, **W** how many machines must hold a write before "ok", **R** how many you ask on a read, and **the conflict rule** decides what happens when copies disagree. Real configs: Dynamo's common (N, R, W) of (3, 2, 2); R = 1, W = N for read-heavy catalogs; Cassandra QUORUM with QUORUM.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: A common misconception: "security owns security risk". In every framework in this course, the **business owner** of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it. The security team advises, measures and challenges. When security silently accepts risk on the business's behalf, nobody with budget or authority knows the risk exists.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: Every risk ends in one of four decisions, recorded with an owner and a date. Compare options in money: expected yearly loss plus treatment cost for the average, and tail percentiles for survival. Mitigation usually wins on average; insurance wins on the tail; avoidance can win on both.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
md: PCI DSS is a contractual standard with 12 requirements. Scope is the CDE plus anything connected to it or able to affect it, so reduce scope first: segment, and better, never touch card numbers (tokenise with a payment provider). What remains on your side, especially the payment page's scripts, must be inventoried and watched.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
md: Policies: short, owned, true, enforced by guardrails, with an exception path and a review date. Awareness: required by every framework, but measure it honestly; put the weight on controls that make human mistakes survivable, and on making reporting easy.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC study of DeepCAM (a deep learning model that finds extreme weather patterns in climate images), a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Build, load and test a Rust module
md: Misconception: "an `assert!` in a kernel doctest panics the kernel." In doctests and `#[kunit_tests]` modules the assert macros are replaced with versions that report to KUnit and do not panic. That is also why tests should use `?` instead of `unwrap()`: an `unwrap()` on `Err` is a real panic, and the kernel's panic handler calls `BUG()`, which reports a fatal kernel error (more in lesson 3).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: EEVDF in one line: weight sets the share, the requested slice sets the latency, and eligibility keeps any task from running far ahead of its share. A BPF scheduler gets none of this for free; lesson 5 shows the minimal one getting weights only partly right.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: A scheduler is two programs: a BPF object (callbacks plus maps, gathered in one `sched_ext_ops` struct_ops map) and a loader that opens it, sets read-only options, loads, attaches, polls and reports why it exited. Exiting the loader is the unload.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Measure percentiles, not means; A/B on one kernel, alternating runs, and report the spread. Then verify the nice and cgroup controls you depend on, because each scheduler decides which ones it honors.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
md: Rotation that nobody watches fails silently. Alert on rotation failures, on keys older than their cryptoperiod, and on authentication failures right after a rotation (a consumer that missed the switch). The Storm-0558 key in the next lesson survived because rotation had stopped and nothing alerted on its age.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: archives, asserts, temp files and what Bandit sees
md: Python review checklist from lessons 3 and 4: no eval/exec/pickle/unsafe YAML on outside data; archive extraction with filter='data' and size limits; no assert for security; mkstemp or NamedTemporaryFile, never mktemp; secrets for tokens and compare_digest for comparisons; and a manual trace for every path.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
md: When reviewing C control flow, read the braces, not the indentation, and ask: if this function exits early, what does it return? A security check must fail closed: the only path to "success" should be the one that passed every check.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
md: A finding is complete when a developer can act on it alone: what is wrong (line and CWE), why it matters (impact and who can reach it), how you know (a safe reproduction), how to fix the class (code), and how to keep it fixed (a regression test that fails on the old code).

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
md: The bug was not "MD5 is old" alone. It was MD5 in a construction that let a collision survive the secret (secret at the end), plus a protocol rule that let the attacker plant bytes inside the authenticated reply. Keyed constructions like HMAC, and authenticating the whole channel with TLS, remove both.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
md: "EAL4 certified" on a datasheet tells you how hard the evaluators looked, not what they looked at. The answer to "certified for what?" is in the security target, and it may exclude the very feature you are buying the product for.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
md: SASE is a delivery model, not a new control. Underneath it are the same enforcement points as before (firewall, web filter, CASB, ZTNA), moved from your data centre to someone else's points of presence.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLM-assisted triage: the model advises, code and people decide
md: A suggestion field that accepts free text will eventually contain an action, a threat or an instruction. Constrain it to a fixed set of values and treat everything else as a failed reply.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: Vulnerability = the weakness. Threat = who or what could use it. Exploit = the act or code that uses it. Payload = what runs afterwards. Risk = likelihood times impact. You remove risk by fixing vulnerabilities, reducing exposure, or reducing impact (backups, and segmentation: splitting a network into zones that cannot freely reach each other).

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
md: Equifax failed at the boring basics: inventory, patch tracking, credential storage, segmentation and monitoring health. No single failure caused the breach; every layer had a hole, which is the subject of lesson 10.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
md: Hedging is not the same as honesty. "May potentially" hides uncertainty instead of stating it. If you are unsure, say what you know, what you do not, and how sure you are (the incident lesson later in this course gives you the words). If you are sure, do not hedge to sound modest.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
md: Turning off DTDs (DOCTYPE declarations) removes the whole feature: no DTD, no entity declarations, so no external entity fetch and no billion laughs. OWASP's first rule is to disable DTDs whenever possible, and to keep XInclude off too, since it loads documents without any DTD. If a format truly needs DTDs, disable external entities and external DTD loading explicitly, and keep the parser library up to date.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
md: Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
md: Do not ask people to detect lies in real time. Give them a rule that does not depend on the caller being honest, and make following the rule faster than arguing.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
md: The people layer is defended by design (processes that do not depend on spotting lies), by technology that makes mistakes harmless, and by a culture where reporting is fast, safe and thanked. Blame breaks all three.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Negative weights mean an ordinary kriging estimate can fall outside the range of the readings. That can be right for a smooth field with a peak between sensors, but for quantities that must stay positive (rainfall, concentrations) check for negative predictions.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
md: Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Thread caches are a memory-for-speed trade. jemalloc's manual says it plainly: caching makes allocation very fast but increases memory use and fragmentation, since some objects stay parked in each thread's cache. TCMalloc moved to per-CPU caches because per-thread caches made footprint grow with the number of threads.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Little free memory is not a problem by itself. The page cache deliberately fills idle RAM with file data, and clean cached pages are reclaimable at any moment. Trouble shows up as rates: sustained swap-in and swap-out in `vmstat`, major faults per second, and processes stalled in direct reclaim.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: Teacher forcing is a training trick. At inference the decoder only ever sees its own earlier outputs, mistakes included, and the encoder output is computed once per source sentence, not once per step.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
md: BM25 = sum over query terms of IDF x f / (f + k1 x (1 - b + b x |d| / avgdl)). Three statistics per term and document: f, |d|, and n_t; two per collection: N and avgdl.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: A density value is not a probability, so it can be larger than 1. A density squeezed onto a narrow range must be tall to keep its total area at 1: spread evenly over an interval of width 0.5, its height is 2. Only areas under a density are probabilities.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
md: The Hessian holds the curvature in every direction. Its eigenvalues classify a critical point (all positive: minimum; mixed signs: saddle), the largest one sets the stable learning rate $2/\lambda_{\max}$, and their ratio sets how slowly gradient descent converges.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: Inside `[ ]`, quote every variable: `[ "$x" = foo ]`. An empty or spaced value otherwise changes how many arguments `[` receives, and the test fails with an error instead of returning false. Inside `[[ ]]` a variable needs no quotes, except on the right of `==` or `=~`: there quotes make the pattern literal, so `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file named `*.log`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
md: Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: Compile each `.c` file separately into a `.o`, then link them. The preprocessor pastes text, the compiler checks one translation unit at a time, and the linker joins units together by symbol name.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Narrow types promote to int before arithmetic; mixed signed and unsigned operands usually become unsigned; conversion to unsigned wraps modulo 2 to the width. Compile with `-Wall -Wextra` and read every sign warning.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Check every return value from a library call. On failure, errno says why; perror and strerror turn it into text. Release resources on every path, typically through one cleanup label, and report the outcome through the exit status.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: A lifetime parameter on a struct marks it as a view into data it does not own, and the checker keeps every use of the view inside the data's lifetime. Return `&'a T` from a method to tie the result to the data rather than to the struct.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches
md: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$: eigenvectors are the directions $A$ only stretches, eigenvalues the stretch factors, found from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. Repeated multiplication is dominated by the largest $|\lambda|$. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors: $S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
md: Gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L$. On a quadratic, each step multiplies the error by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per direction, so it converges only if $\eta < 2/\lambda$ for every curvature $\lambda$, and the sharpest direction sets the limit.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: Expected test error = bias squared + variance + noise. Simple models miss systematically (bias), flexible models chase noise (variance), and the noise sets a floor nobody can beat. Regularization and more data mainly cut variance.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
md: A complete training loop is: split, fit preprocessing on train, shuffle each epoch, step on minibatch gradients plus the penalty gradient, watch validation loss, keep the best weights, and evaluate on test once. Every bug in later, bigger models is a violation of one of these steps.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form
md: A batched gradient is the per-example gradient summed (or averaged) over the rows of the batch. The transposes are just how a matrix product writes that sum, and a quick check that every gradient has the shape of its parameter catches most mistakes.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
md: No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: Most concurrency bugs are atomicity violations (fix: a lock around the whole check-then-act) or order violations (fix: a condition variable on a state variable). Deadlock needs four conditions; the usual cure is to acquire locks in one global order.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: The mean answers "total divided by count", the median answers "what is typical", and tail percentiles answer "how bad is it for the unlucky few". For skewed data, report more than the mean.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: The CDF turns any range question into a subtraction, $F(b) - F(a)$. Standardizing turns any normal question into the standard normal CDF, $\Phi$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 3), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size (here the 2 point gap) and its confidence interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler, which never puts the same text twice in one batch, for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: Initialization is about **variance, not values**. Pick the weight scale so that each layer multiplies the activation variance (and the gradient variance) by about 1. For ReLU that means $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/\text{fan-in}$; with depth, any other factor compounds exponentially.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
md: Every stage is a trust boundary, and attackers pick the stage with the widest fan-out: one poisoned library, build server or CI action reaches thousands of victims at once. Defence means asking, for each arrow, what proves the thing arriving is the thing you expected.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
md: Provenance moves the question from 'do I trust this file?' to 'do I trust this repository, this workflow and this build platform?', which you can check by machine. npm's documentation is explicit that provenance does not guarantee a package has no malicious code; it makes origin verifiable.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: To share writable memory, both processes need `MAP_SHARED` mappings of the same pages: anonymous before `fork`, a `shm_open` name, or a memfd descriptor. Then order the accesses with release and acquire atomics or a lock; the mapping itself guarantees no ordering at all.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
md: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, not a replacement for the first. It pays most when the model can already sometimes solve the task and something can recognize a correct answer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Large-chunk TTT, one map of the design space, and the costs
md: Learned memory turns the state of a recurrent layer into a model trained online. You choose its architecture, objective, forgetting and optimizer; you pay for expressiveness in wall-clock time, and you still pair it with attention for exact local recall.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Three ways to start a hunt: hypothesis, intelligence and data
md: A hypothesis that cannot fail is not a hypothesis. "Something bad may be happening somewhere" will consume a week and conclude nothing. Name the behaviour, the place and the data. A disproved hypothesis is a useful result: it is evidence that one specific attack path is not in use, at least in the data you have.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
md: Threat intelligence is threat information that has been analysed and put in context **for a decision**. If you cannot name the decision a product supports, you are not yet producing intelligence.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Sharing at machine speed: TAXII, MISP and communities
md: Automated sharing amplifies errors as fast as it spreads truth. Before publishing, check values against warning lists, set `to_ids` only on values safe to block, add an expiry or decay model, and never publish an indicator you have not graded.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE per element: from a diagram to a threat list
md: STRIDE per element checks parts, not their combination. The 2006 article admits that threats frequently materialise only when systems are joined, because combining them violates assumptions each part made. Always ask what changes when this system is connected to the next one.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
md: Tiering wins only if the *hot* pages live in the fast tier. The capacity of each tier matters less than the fraction of accesses it serves. Everything in this course is machinery for keeping $h$ high cheaply.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins
md: Report a forecast's accuracy as an average over many origins, at the horizon you will use in production, with a scaled metric such as MASE next to seasonal naive. A single train/test split can rank two methods either way by luck.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
md: Domain validation proves control of a name at one moment, nothing more. Anyone who can control your DNS or your web server's port 80 for a few minutes can get a valid certificate for your domain. That is why CAA, multi-perspective validation and CT monitoring exist.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: Fusion in Triton is mostly a matter of keeping a tile in registers between operations. Load once, do every elementwise op and reduction on the block, store once.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: GenEval prompts are short and templated, and some models are trained mostly on long synthetic captions. Emu3's authors say exactly this and report rewriter numbers too. Before comparing two papers, check the rewriter, the CFG scale, and whether numbers were measured or copied from another paper.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
md: A unikernel runs many requests on one vCPU by **interleaving at waits**: an event loop or cooperative threads overlap I/O, a long computation blocks everyone, and more cores means **more unikernels**, not more threads.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
md: SIMD kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar loop. FAISS explicitly allows reassociation in its distance loops; that is a deliberate choice, not a bug. Do not assert exact equality of distances across CPUs or builds.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
md: Do not read `world_size` as the data-parallel size. On 8 GPUs with TP 2 a WorkerGroup has 8 workers but only 4 data shards. Splitting the batch 8 ways would hand different samples to two GPUs that must run the same sharded matmul together.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
md: pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
md: A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the image at full resolution. It sees whatever grid the encoder produced. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo squeezed into 336 x 336 loses most of its pixels before the language model ever runs.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
md: The progress ladder, weakest to strongest: **blocking** (a stalled lock holder can stop everyone), **lock-free** (some thread always completes), **wait-free** (every thread completes in finitely many of its own steps), **bounded wait-free** (every thread completes within a fixed number of its own steps).

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: An MLWP model learns one function: global state now (a tensor of about 10^8 numbers) to global state a few hours later, supervised by reanalysis.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Mapping the application: entry points, roles and workflows
md: Test the requests, not the pages. Every entry point gets a row: method, path template, parameters, roles, state change, object ids. That table drives everything that follows.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Chaining low findings into real impact
md: Rate findings by what they let an attacker do next, and prove chains with your own accounts up to the first step that shows the end state. Defenders: one broken link breaks the chain, so fix the cheap links.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookies, sessions, and how Firesheep hijacked them in 2010
md: A session cookie is a **bearer token**: whoever bears (holds) it is, as far as the server is concerned, the logged-in user. No password is needed to use it. Protecting the session ID matters as much as protecting the password, for as long as the session is valid.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
md: Practise only on machines you own or are allowed to test, ideally a Windows virtual machine you created. The legal line from security-basics applies to every command and tool in this course.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why wireless is different: a medium anyone in range can hear
md: Wireless security starts from one assumption: an attacker in radio range receives every frame, and can transmit frames of their own. Only cryptography (encryption plus authentication of every frame and of the network itself) changes what they can do with that position.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
md: iOS security is layered: signed code only, every app sandboxed, entitlements signed in, memory mitigations, keys in a separate Secure Enclave, files encrypted per class, and the riskiest parsers isolated in BlastDoor. Real attacks (lesson 17) need a chain of bugs to get through several layers.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS
md: Owner and thieves only ever race for the last task. Every other take is a store, a fence and a load with no CAS, and a push needs no read-modify-write at all.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Other ways to drop the end date: averaging, schedule-free, theory
md: A cooldown, a checkpoint average and Schedule-Free's running average all do the same job: they stop the high-LR bouncing from showing in the weights you evaluate. They differ in what they cost (extra steps, extra copies, retuning) and in whether the training run must know its end date.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Common failure modes: modifying a buffer or file before the kernel is done with it (silent corruption on the wire), forgetting to drain the error queue (pinned memory grows until ENOBUFS), benchmarking over loopback (always copied), and assuming a notification means the peer received the data.
